client: I’ve been struggling a lot since I got my diagnosis. It’s like my mind won’t stop racing—I’m always worrying about what’s going to happen next or if things will get worse. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help because it feels like this anxiety is just… part of me now.
therapist: It sounds like receiving this diagnosis has left you feeling overwhelmed with racing thoughts and uncertainty about the future. I hear how exhausting it must be to carry this constant worry. Would you be willing to share what thoughts come up most often when your mind starts racing like this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, it's like my brain won't shut off. I keep thinking "What if the treatment doesn't work?" or "How will I handle work if things get worse?" The worst part is imagining my family having to take care of me - that makes me feel so guilty. 

I know I should stay positive, but it's hard when my mind jumps to worst-case scenarios all the time. Even when I try to distract myself, the thoughts creep back in.
therapist: I can hear how much these "what if" thoughts are weighing on you, especially when they involve your loved ones. That sense of guilt about burdening others seems particularly painful. Have you noticed if these thoughts follow any particular patterns or triggers throughout your day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I notice the "what if" thoughts get worse in the evenings when I'm alone with my thoughts. During the day I can distract myself with work, but at night it's like my brain won't shut off about all the ways I might be disappointing people. Part of me knows I'm probably overthinking, but it still feels so real in the moment. 

I guess the biggest trigger is when someone close to me seems even slightly distant - like if my partner doesn't text back right away, my brain immediately jumps to "what if they're tired of dealing with me?" It's exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like evenings have become particularly challenging, when the quiet makes space for these painful thoughts about disappointing others. I notice you describe this experience vividly, yet there's also a part of you recognizing these might be overthinking patterns. Would it help to explore what happens physically in your body when these "what if" thoughts about your partner arise?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I do notice my chest gets really tight when those thoughts come up, like I can't take a full breath. But I don't know if focusing on that will help - it just makes me more aware of how anxious I feel, you know? Sometimes I think maybe I should just distract myself instead of paying attention to the physical stuff.
therapist: I hear how uncomfortable it feels when you notice that tightness in your chest, and how tempting it is to push those sensations away. It makes sense that you'd want to distract yourself when the physical feelings of anxiety become so intense. Would you be open to exploring together how we might approach these physical sensations with curiosity rather than fear?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about approaching the anxiety with curiosity, but honestly that sounds terrifying. When my chest gets tight, all I can think is "something bad is about to happen" - how am I supposed to just observe that calmly? It feels like my body is warning me about real danger.
therapist: It's completely understandable that this idea feels terrifying right now - your body's alarm system is sounding very real warnings to you. That sense of impending danger is so visceral when anxiety takes hold. Perhaps we could start smaller - would you feel comfortable just noticing how long these physical sensations typically last when they occur?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know...when the anxiety hits, it feels like it lasts forever. Even if I try to time it, I get so caught up in the panic that I lose track. And honestly, focusing on the physical sensations makes me more aware of them, which just makes the anxiety worse.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming it feels when the anxiety takes hold, and how trying to track it seems to intensify the experience rather than help. That makes complete sense - when we're in distress, our natural instinct is to resist or escape the discomfort. Would it feel safer to explore other grounding techniques that don't involve focusing directly on the physical sensations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I'm willing to try something different, but I'm skeptical. Every time I've tried breathing exercises or grounding techniques before, my mind just races even more. It feels like putting a bandaid on something that needs stitches, you know? The anxiety always seems to break through anyway.
therapist: I appreciate your honesty about feeling skeptical - it makes sense that previous attempts with breathing exercises might have felt inadequate when the anxiety feels so deep. That "bandaid versus stitches" comparison really shows how overwhelming this experience has been for you. What if we approached this differently by first understanding what makes those techniques feel ineffective for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess what makes the breathing exercises feel ineffective is that they don’t really address the root of my anxiety—they just feel like a distraction. When I’m in the middle of a panic attack, it’s hard to even remember to breathe deeply because my thoughts are racing so fast. It’s like trying to put out a fire with a cup of water.
therapist: Your frustration makes complete sense - when the anxiety feels like an overwhelming fire, simple breathing can understandably seem insufficient. I hear how the racing thoughts make it nearly impossible to even access those coping tools in the moment. Would it help if we worked on developing some strategies that feel more connected to addressing those deeper worries you mentioned earlier?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess that could help... but I don't know. Those deeper worries feel so real and justified to me. Like when I'm anxious about failing at work, it's not just in my head - my boss actually has high expectations. Wouldn't ignoring those realities just make things worse?
therapist: I hear how important it is for you to acknowledge these very real work pressures - we're certainly not suggesting ignoring those valid concerns. What if we explored ways to address both the external pressures and your internal response to them, so you don't have to choose between recognizing reality and managing your anxiety?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you acknowledging the work pressures are real - sometimes I worry therapy will just tell me to "think positive" and ignore the actual problems. But I'm not sure how to separate the external stress from my anxiety about it - they feel so tangled together right now. When I try to manage my reactions, it almost feels like I'm pretending the workload isn't crushing me.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two important truths here - the real work pressures you're facing, and the way your anxiety amplifies them. That tangled feeling makes complete sense when you're dealing with both external demands and internal distress. Would it help if we explored how to validate the real challenges while also finding ways to prevent them from becoming overwhelming?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
